implementation_notes: Ruby needs no abstract hook: any object that responds to #update satisfies the pattern, so entities.each { |e| e.update(dt) } is hook, collection and driver at once, with a shared module or a documented contract stating the requirement. What replaces the classic structure: duck typing replaces the abstract base class and the standard Array replaces the entity manager; Gosu supplies only the window-level frame callback ('This method is called once every update_interval milliseconds while the window is being shown'), so the per-object walk inside it is yours. An explicit class hierarchy is only worth it when entities share substantial implementation - otherwise it is ceremony Ruby does not need.
code_sketch:
class Guard
  def initialize = @x = 0.0
  def update(dt) = @x += 20.0 * dt        # the hook (any object may have one)
end

class World
  def initialize = @entities = [Guard.new]
  def update(dt) = @entities.each { |e| e.update(dt) }   # the driver walk
end
pitfalls: Duck typing has no compile-time check: an object without #update raises NoMethodError mid-frame, so define a shared module or a documented contract and test the collection.
Mutating the array during each (delete/<<) skips or double-processes elements; iterate a dup, then reject dead entries after the walk.
Per-call overhead and the GVL make thousands of Ruby-level update calls the bottleneck: hoist instance-variable lookups into locals and profile before optimising.
each returns the receiver, so entities = entities.each { ... } looks like it transforms state but does not; prefer plain each plus filter after the walk in hot code.
